findings.who: A parent whose child disappeared for a few days or weeks in 2025 and was thought at the time to be a runaway or lost, then came home. Only later, possibly after 2025, did police presume an abduction by a stranger. The child is a non-relative or other household member whose dependency rests on living with the filer all year.
findings.why_no: The gate's help says to answer No only 'for a child who was missing because of a kidnapping'. The filer did not think of the episode as a kidnapping when it happened, or does not know of the later presumption. They also read the help's list of absences (vacation, hospital) as covering a short time away. So they answer Yes to 'live with you for all of 2025'. The gated question's own help ('Answer Yes even if the authorities first presumed the kidnapping after 2025') is never shown to them.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 18, Kidnapped child: 'You can treat a child as your qualifying relative even if the child has been kidnapped ... 1. The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family.'
findings.fix: Change the gate help to: 'If the child was missing at any time in 2025, even briefly, answer No, including when the police presumed a kidnapping only later or the child has since come home.'

findings.who: A married filer files separately. The child lived with the filer, the spouse (the child's other parent) and the filer's mother all year. The child is a qualifying child of both the spouse and the grandparent.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the spouse is the 'only other person' the child could be the qualifying child of. Because the grandparent also qualifies, the truthful answer is no. The tool then never asks whether the spouse will claim the child, even though the spouse is still a competing claimant.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 15: "If the parents don't file a joint return together but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived for the longer period of time during the year."
findings.fix: Gate on 'Is your husband or wife one of the people this child could be the qualifying child of (whether or not anyone else could be)?' Ask about the spouse's claim whenever that is yes. Handle the other persons in a separate question.

findings.who: A married filer files separately and has custody. The spouse is the noncustodial parent and lived apart from the child for most of the year. The filer signed Form 8332, or a pre-2009 decree applies, so the spouse can claim the child under the divorced or separated parents rule.
findings.why_no: The child did not live with the spouse for more than half the year. So the filer truthfully says the child could not be the spouse's 'qualifying child'. Under the release, though, the spouse can still claim the child as a dependent and take the child tax credit.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 17: "If a child is treated as the qualifying child of the noncustodial parent under the rules ... for children of divorced or separated parents (or parents who live apart), only the noncustodial parent can claim the child as a dependent and claim the child tax credit, additional child tax credit, or credit for other dependents for the child."
findings.fix: Before the qualifying-child gate, ask: 'Have you signed Form 8332 or a similar release, or does a decree let your husband or wife claim this child?' Route a yes to the spouse-claims question, or to its own refusal.

findings.who: A married filer files separately. The spouse moved out in August, and the child lived with each parent for more than half the year, as in p501 Example 6.
findings.why_no: The filer cannot apply the residency, support, age and joint return tests to the spouse. Because the spouse moved out, the filer assumes the child is 'my' qualifying child only and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 17, Example 6: "Your child is a qualifying child of both you and your spouse because your child lived with each of you for more than half the year"; Example 7: "only your spouse will be allowed to treat your child as a qualifying child."
findings.fix: Ask facts the filer can check: 'Did this child live with your husband or wife for more than half of 2025 (time living with you both counts)?' Derive qualifying-child status from that answer instead of asking for the classification.

findings.who: A married filer files separately. The child is the filer's own child and the spouse's stepchild, and the child lived with both of them all year.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'could be the qualifying child of' as meaning the child's parent. They do not count a stepparent, so they answer no. The tiebreaker definition of 'parent', which excludes stepparents, reinforces that reading. But a stepchild still meets the relationship test for a qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 17, Step 1: "A qualifying child is your... Son, daughter, stepchild, foster child..."; p501 p. 15: "generally only one person can actually treat the child as a qualifying child"
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Count your husband or wife even if they are the child's stepparent or foster parent, or related as a sibling or other relative, if the child lived with them for more than half the year.'

locators: p. 17, Step 1, "If the child meets the conditions to be a qualifying child of any other person (other than your spouse if filing jointly) for 2025, see Qualifying child of more than one person, later."

p. 15, Tiebreaker rules, "but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived for the longer period of time during the year"; p. 17, "Subject to these tiebreaker rules, you and the other person may be able to choose which of you claims the child as a qualifying child."
p. 17, "Subject to these tiebreaker rules, you and the other person may be able to choose which of you claims the child as a qualifying child."

findings.who: A qualifying surviving spouse whose qualifying person is a stepchild, for example the deceased spouse's son, who lived with the filer all year. On the dependent's "Relationship to you" question, the filer picks "stepchild" (or "stepson"), not "child".
findings.why_no: The gate requires the relationship helper to equal exactly 'child'. A filer who truthfully picks a separate stepchild option makes the gate false, so the tool never asks own_child and sets the line to false. The helper's coding of stepchildren is not shown.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15, Qualifying Surviving Spouse: "2. You have a child or stepchild (not a foster child) whom you can claim as a dependent"
findings.fix: Open the gate for every relationship value that can be a son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child or child placed for adoption (for example relationship in {child, son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child, other} when QSS is checked). Or ask own_child for every dependent on a QSS return and let the question itself sort out foster children and grandchildren.

findings.who: A qualifying surviving spouse with a child lawfully placed for legal adoption in 2025, adoption not yet final. The filer records the relationship as "other", "foster/placed child" or "not yet my child".
findings.why_no: Before finalization, the filer does not see the child as their "child". The relationship helper never reaches 'child', so the gate is false. The help that would correct this ("one placed with you for adoption is your son or daughter") appears only behind the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15: "Adopted child. An adopted child is always treated as your own child. An adopted child includes a child lawfully placed with you for legal adoption."
findings.fix: State in the help for the relationship question that a child placed with you for legal adoption counts as your child. Or open the gate on any non-foster relationship when QSS is checked.

findings.who: A qualifying surviving spouse whose child is not claimed as a dependent: the child had gross income of $5,200 or more, the child filed a joint return, or the filer can be claimed on someone else's return. The child is entered only in the filing-status entry space, not in the Dependents section.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for a person "Listed as your child" in the dependent document. A child who truthfully is not a listed dependent has no dependent entry, so the gate is never true for that child. Test 2 is then never confirmed through this line, which may lead to a wrong refusal of the filing status, or none.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15: "whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except that, for 2025: a. The child had gross income of $5,200 or more, b. The child filed a joint return, or c. You could be claimed as a dependent on someone else's return. If the child isn't claimed as your dependent, enter the child's name in the entry space."
findings.fix: Ask own_child, and record the child, at the household level for the QSS qualifying child, whether or not the child is listed as a dependent. Or add a non-claimed QSS child record that opens the same question.

findings.who: A parent filing Form 8814 for a dependent child whose interest/dividends exceed $1,350, so the parent reports the child’s income and the child is not required to file a separate return.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether the dependent is required to file because of income. Because the Form 8814 election means the child need not file, the parent truthfully answers no; the gate never asks for the Worksheet 1-2 amount.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 8, Line 2b and Worksheet 1-2: “If you are filing Form 8814 ... and the amount on Form 8814, line 4, is more than $1,350, you must include on line 1 of Worksheet 1-2 the sum of the tax-exempt interest from Form 8814, line 1b; the lesser of Form 8814, line 4 or line 5; and any nontaxable social security benefits your child received.”
findings.fix: Make the gate true when Form 8814 is filed and line 4 exceeds $1,350, and ask for the Worksheet 1-2 amounts from Form 8814 even if the child is not required to file.

findings.who: An unmarried dependent under 65 and not blind with $15,000 earned income and $1,000 unearned income. Neither quoted threshold is exceeded, but gross income is $16,000, more than the larger of $1,350 or earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450 ($15,450).
findings.why_no: The help/citation quotes only “Your unearned income was over $1,350” and “Your earned income was over $15,750.” Reading that list as complete, the dependent answers no because neither bullet applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 10, Chart B: “Your gross income was more than the larger of— $1,350, or Your earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.”
findings.fix: Show the full Chart B gross-income test, not just the unearned and earned threshold bullets, or ask directly whether gross income exceeds the larger of $1,350 or earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.

findings.who: A married couple files jointly. The child is the wife's biological child and the husband's stepchild, and the husband is the one entering the dependents.
findings.why_no: The help for relationship tells him to answer for himself, so he picks child (stepchild). The gated question asks 'Are you this child's parent', and its help says 'A stepparent ... who has not adopted the child answers No.' He truthfully answers No, which may end the interview, although his spouse on the same joint return is the biological parent.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 21: 'If the parents file a joint return together and can claim the child as a qualifying child, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parents.' p501 p. 19: 'If you file a joint return, the person can be related to either you or your spouse.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Are you or your spouse (if filing jointly) this child's parent by birth or by adoption?' In the help, say that on a joint return a stepparent answers Yes when the spouse is the child's parent by birth or adoption.

findings.who: An aunt, uncle, older sibling or other relative has legally adopted a niece, nephew or younger sibling, as in a kinship adoption after a parent died or lost custody.
findings.why_no: The relationship question and its help give no rule for adoption. The filer gives the blood relationship (sibling, or sibling's child) instead of child, so the gated question is never asked and the line is false. The IRS treats an adopted child as the filer's own child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'Adopted child. An adopted child is always treated as your own child.' p501 p. 19: '(A legally adopted child is considered your child.)'
findings.fix: Add to the relationship help: 'If you adopted this person, or the person was lawfully placed with you for adoption, choose child, even if they are also your niece, nephew, brother, sister or grandchild by birth.'

findings.who: A filer whose child was lawfully placed with them for legal adoption by an agency or court, but the adoption was not final by the end of 2025.
findings.why_no: The question says 'by adoption', and the help names a 'foster parent ... who has not adopted the child' as answering No. A filer whose adoption is still pending reads that as meaning they have not adopted yet and answers No. The IRS counts a child lawfully placed for adoption as an adopted child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: 'An adopted child includes a child lawfully placed with you for legal adoption.' p501 p. 19: 'The term "adopted child" includes a child who was lawfully placed with you for legal adoption.'
findings.fix: Add to the gated help: 'Answer Yes if the child was lawfully placed with you for legal adoption, even if the adoption is not yet final.'

findings.who: A biological parent whose child was born of a relationship that broke local law, such as a bigamous marriage or a relationship with someone married to another person.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Choose the last answer if your relationship with the person broke local law.' The parent reads 'relationship' as the relationship the child came from and picks the last answer (other) instead of child. The gated question is then skipped.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 19: 'Local law violated. A person doesn't meet this test if at any time during the year the relationship between you and that person violates local law.' i1040gi p. 21: 'the term "parent" means a biological or adoptive parent of an individual.'
findings.fix: Reword the help: 'Choose the last answer only for a person who is not related to you and whose relationship with you (for example, living together) broke local law. Your own child, stepchild or foster child is always child.'
